# Where we left off, and where we're going

## Last session, in one line {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Small rules build big patterns
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Today's big pattern: a single number that summarises what happened to thousands of
prices at once.
:::

## How today works {.center}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We follow one book, in order. *A Practical Introduction to Index Numbers* by Ralph,
O'Neill and Winton.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Every idea is built up step by step, with a worked example, before we look at any
formula.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
At the end, we test all of it against a real case. India's CPI, and what happened to
it during the COVID-19 lockdown.
:::

::: {.incremental}
1. Chapter 1. What is an index number.
2. Chapter 2. Index numbers and change.
3. Chapter 4. Introducing price and quantity.

# Part 1: Chapter 1, What Is an Index Number

## 1.1 What is an index number? {.center}

## A company's sales, year after year

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Here is the total value of retail sales in Great Britain, in billions of pounds.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Year | Sales (£bn) |
|---|---|
| 2005 | 281.450 |
| 2006 | 292.110 |
| 2007 | 303.621 |
| 2008 | 321.178 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Sales are clearly rising. But how much easier would it be to read that change if we
did not have to do the arithmetic ourselves?
:::

## Pick a year to compare everything to

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Choose one year as your reference point. Call it the **base period**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Let's choose 2005.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Now give 2005 a clean, memorable value. Not £281.450 billion. Just **100**.
:::

## Rescaling the series {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:80px; font-size:1.6em;"}
2005: £281.450bn becomes **100**
:::

## Rescaling the series {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:60px; font-size:1.4em;"}
2005: £281.450bn becomes **100**
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; margin-top:30px; font-size:1.4em;"}
Every other year is scaled by the same factor.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; margin-top:20px; font-size:1.4em;"}
2006: £292.110bn becomes **103.79**
:::

## The rescaled series

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Year | Sales (£bn) | Index (2005 = 100) |
|---|---|---|
| 2005 | 281.450 | 100.00 |
| 2006 | 292.110 | 103.79 |
| 2007 | 303.621 | 107.88 |
| 2008 | 321.178 | 114.12 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This rescaled column is a set of **index numbers**. Now the change is readable at a
glance.
:::

## Reading the index number

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Look at 2007. The index value is **107.88**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
That single number tells you sales were **7.88% higher** in 2007 than in 2005.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
You did not need a calculator to see that. The scaling did the work for you.
:::

## What did we gain, and what did we lose?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We gained a direct, readable measure of **change**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We lost the actual monetary values. The index alone does not tell you sales were
£303.621 billion in 2007.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
That trade-off is usually worth it. Often we care about the *change* far more than
the *level*.
:::

## 1.2 Example: the Consumer Prices Index {.center}

## From sales to prices

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The same rescaling idea applies to prices. This gives us the **Consumer Prices
Index**, or CPI.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The CPI tracks the general level of prices of consumer goods and services, month by
month.
:::

## Reading a real CPI table

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Month | Index (2005 = 100) | 1-month rate | 12-month rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sep 2012 | 123.5 | 0.4 | 2.2 |
| Oct 2012 | 124.2 | 0.5 | 2.7 |
| Nov 2012 | 124.4 | 0.2 | 2.7 |
| Dec 2012 | 125.0 | 0.5 | 2.7 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
In September 2012, prices were 23.5% above their 2005 level.
:::

## Checking the 1-month rate ourselves

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The 1-month rate compares each month only to the **one before it**, using the same
percentage change formula from Chapter 2.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$g^{s,t} = \frac{I^{0,t} - I^{0,s}}{I^{0,s}} \times 100$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
November's index was 124.4. December's was 125.0.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$\frac{125.0 - 124.4}{124.4} \times 100 = 0.48\% \approx 0.5\%$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This matches the table. The 12-month rate works the same way, just compared to the
same month a year earlier instead of the month before.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="border-left: 6px solid #b03; padding-left: 20px;"}
A caution: try this with September to October instead, and you get 0.6%, not the
0.5% shown. The published rate is calculated from **unrounded** source data, then
rounded for display, separately from the index values themselves. Recalculating from
the rounded index can occasionally land one tenth of a point off.
:::

## The number that actually matters

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Here is a subtlety worth sitting with. The **level** of the CPI is not published as
a headline figure, and it is not very informative on its own.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
It is the **rate of change**, the 12-month rate, that is the headline statistic.
That rate of change is what we call **inflation**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is why inflation, not "the price level," leads the news every month.
:::

## How the CPI is actually built, in one sentence

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A representative **basket** of about 700 goods and services is chosen.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
About 180,000 individual prices are collected for these items every month, across a
sample of shops and locations.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We will unfold exactly how these prices get combined into one number later today.
:::

## 1.3 Example: FTSE 100 {.center}

## A different kind of index

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The **FTSE 100** tracks the share prices of the 100 largest companies listed on the
London Stock Exchange.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Each company's share price counts more or less depending on the company's size, its
**market capitalisation**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
It is updated every 15 seconds during trading hours.
:::

## An important twist: the base need not be 100

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The FTSE 100 was first produced in 1984. Its starting value was not 100.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.r-fit-text}
It started at **1000**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
There is no strict rule that the base value must be 100. It is simply a convenient,
common choice. The FTSE 100 has since risen past 6000, several times its starting
value.
:::

## 1.4 Example: the Multidimensional Poverty Index {.center}

## Combining things that are not prices at all

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
So far, every index combined quantities of the **same type**. Pounds of sales,
prices of goods.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
What if the things you want to combine are not even measured in the same units?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is called a **composite indicator**. The Multidimensional Poverty Index, or
MPI, is a classic example.
:::

## What goes into the MPI

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Dimension | Indicator | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Health | Child mortality | 1/6 |
| Health | Health | 1/6 |
| Education | Years of schooling | 1/6 |
| Education | Child school attendance | 1/6 |
| Living standard | Electricity | 1/18 |
| Living standard | Drinking water | 1/18 |
| Living standard | Sanitation, flooring, cooking fuel, assets | 1/18 each |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Ten very different indicators, each with a weight, combined into one poverty score
per country.
:::

## 1.5 Example: the Gender Inequality Index {.center}

## A second composite indicator

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The **Gender Inequality Index**, produced by the United Nations, measures inequality
in achievement between men and women.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Dimension | Indicator |
|---|---|
| Health | Maternal mortality ratio |
| Health | Adolescent birth rate |
| Empowerment | Parliamentary representation |
| Empowerment | Educational attainment |
| Labour market | Labour market participation |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Each country gets one overall score, built from five very different indicators.
Countries can then be ranked and compared, across time as well as across countries.
:::

## 1.6 Representing the world with index numbers {.center}

## The upside and the downside

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
On the upside, a single index number can summarise something genuinely complex. That
supports clear communication and policy making.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
On the downside, the same summarising power can flatten a complex reality into a
misleadingly simple number.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A poor underlying model, or poor data, produces a poor indicator, no matter how
official the final number looks.
:::

## The one idea behind every example so far

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Retail sales, the CPI, the FTSE 100, the MPI, the Gender Inequality Index. Five very
different things.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Every single one follows the same construction: raw data, combined according to some
model, into one number.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The rest of today unfolds exactly how that combination is actually done, for prices.
:::

## 1.7 Chapter summary {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- An index number rescales a series so change is easy to read.
- The base period does not have to equal 100, though it usually does.
- The level of an index is often less interesting than its rate of change.
- The same basic idea, combine data into one number, extends far beyond prices.
:::

# Part 2: Chapter 2, Index Numbers and Change

## 2.1 Calculating an index series from a data series {.center}

## Turning the idea into a recipe

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Chapter 1 showed *what* an index number does. Now we build the exact recipe for
*how* to calculate one.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Call the value of something at the base period $x^0$, and its value now, at period
$t$, simply $x^t$.
:::

## Building the formula, step by step {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:100px; font-size:1.6em;"}
Take today's value
:::

## Building the formula, step by step {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:60px; font-size:1.5em;"}
Take today's value, divide by the base period's value
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; margin-top:30px; font-size:1.5em;"}
Multiply by 100
:::

## Building the formula, step by step {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:120px;"}
$$I^{0,t} = 100 \times \frac{x^t}{x^0}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.3em; margin-top:20px;"}
This is the exact formula behind the rescaling we did by hand in Chapter 1.
:::

## Worked example: a company's turnover

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Company A's annual turnover, in £ million, 2002 to 2013.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Year | 2002 | 2003 | 2004 | 2005 | 2006 | 2007 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Turnover | 17.9 | 18.5 | 18.1 | 18.6 | 19.0 | 19.1 |

| Year | 2008 | 2009 | 2010 | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Turnover | 19.3 | 20.2 | 20.3 | 20.0 | 20.5 | 20.4 |
:::

## Calculating the first few index values

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Base period is 2002. So $x^0 = 17.9$.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For 2002 itself: $100 \times \dfrac{17.9}{17.9} = 100.0$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For 2003: $100 \times \dfrac{18.5}{17.9} = 103.4$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For 2012: $100 \times \dfrac{20.5}{17.9} = 114.5$
:::

## The full index series

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Year | 2002 | 2003 | 2004 | 2005 | 2006 | 2007 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Index | 100.0 | 103.4 | 101.1 | 103.9 | 106.1 | 106.7 |

| Year | 2008 | 2009 | 2010 | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Index | 107.8 | 112.8 | 113.4 | 111.7 | 114.5 | 114.0 |
:::

## 2.2 Calculating percentage change {.center}

## Level versus change

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
An index series is really a measure of change. What we usually care about is not
the level of the index, but how much it grew.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The UK's headline figures for GDP and the CPI are both, at heart, reported as
percentage changes in an index series.
:::

## The general percentage change formula {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:100px; font-size:1.6em;"}
(New value minus old value), divided by old value
:::

## The general percentage change formula {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:120px;"}
$$\text{percentage change} = \frac{B - A}{A} \times 100$$
:::

## Applying it to an index series

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Between two periods $s$ and $t$, where $s$ comes before $t$:
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$g^{s,t} = \frac{I^{0,t} - I^{0,s}}{I^{0,s}} \times 100$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
There is a shortcut when comparing back to the base period itself.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$g^{0,t} = I^{0,t} - 100$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is exactly why we chose 100 as the base value. It makes reading percentage
change effortless.
:::

## Worked example: percentage change for Company A

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Using the index series we just built, base period 2002.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- 2002 to 2004: $\dfrac{101.1 - 100}{100} \times 100 = 1.1\%$
- 2002 to 2013: $\dfrac{114.0 - 100}{100} \times 100 = 14.0\%$
- 2005 to 2007: $\dfrac{106.7 - 103.9}{103.9} \times 100 = 2.7\%$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Notice the last one is not a shortcut calculation. Neither period is the base
period, so we need the full formula.
:::

## 2.3 Comparing data series with index numbers {.center}

## A comparison problem

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Suppose we want to compare population growth across the European Union, Germany,
the United Kingdom, and Cyprus, from 1995 to 2011.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The EU's population is roughly 500 million. Cyprus's is under a million. Plotted on
the same raw scale, Cyprus is a flat line near zero.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The raw numbers make comparing *growth rates* almost impossible, even though that is
exactly what we want to compare.
:::

## Rebasing solves it

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Convert all four population series to index numbers, with a common base period,
2000 equals 100.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Now every series starts at the same point, and their *shapes* become directly
comparable.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The result: Cyprus's population rose in percentage terms **more than three times**
as much as the UK's, over this period. A fact the raw population chart completely
hid.
:::

## Why this matters

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Index numbers are not just a display trick. They let us compare things that live on
wildly different scales, fairly, using the same yardstick.
:::

## 2.4 Converting from an index series to a data series {.center}

## The reverse problem

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Sometimes you only have an index series, and you want back the original data. For
example, you might have GDP as an index, but want to know the actual amount in
rupees or pounds.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This needs one more piece of information: the actual data value at any single point
in time.
:::

## Recovering the data {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:100px;"}
$$x^t = \frac{I^{0,t} \times x^s}{I^{0,s}}$$
:::

## Recovering the data {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:60px;"}
$$x^t = \frac{I^{0,t} \times x^s}{I^{0,s}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; margin-top:30px; font-size:1.3em;"}
If the known value happens to be the base period itself, this simplifies:
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.5em;"}
$$x^t = \frac{I^{0,t} \times x^0}{100}$$
:::

## Worked example: recovering turnover

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We are told Company A's turnover in 2006 was exactly **£19.0 million**, and we have
the index series from before. Can we recover every other year?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For 2002: $\dfrac{100.0 \times 19.0}{106.1} = 17.9$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For 2003: $\dfrac{103.4 \times 19.0}{106.1} = 18.5$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Exactly the turnover figures we started with. The index series really does carry
the full shape of the data, just not its scale.
:::

## 2.5 Chapter summary {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- We now have the exact recipe to build an index series from data.
- Percentage change, not the level, is usually the statistic that matters.
- Rebasing to a common base period lets us fairly compare series on different
  scales.
- The recipe also runs backward. An index series plus one known data point recovers
  the whole data series.
:::

## A short gap in the book, before we continue {.center}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Chapter 3 of the book covers the wider range of uses of inflation figures.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We pick the story back up at Chapter 4, where the book asks a sharper question. How
do we build a price index out of *many* items at once?
:::

# Part 3: Chapter 4, Introducing Price and Quantity

## 4.1 Measuring price change {.center}

## Starting as small as possible

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Before measuring price change for an entire economy, start with a single item.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A bottle of washing-up liquid cost **£1.30** in January 2014, and **£1.40** in July
2014.
:::

## Building the price relative {auto-animate="true"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {style="border: 3px solid #444; border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px 40px; text-align: center; font-size: 1.4em;"}
Price now, July
:::
:::

::: {.column width="10%"}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {style="border: 3px solid #444; border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px 40px; text-align: center; font-size: 1.4em;"}
Price then, January
:::
:::
:::

## Building the price relative {auto-animate="true"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {style="border: 3px solid #444; border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px 40px; text-align: center; font-size: 1.4em;"}
£1.40
:::
:::

::: {.column width="16%"}
::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 2em; margin-top: 40px;"}
÷
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {style="border: 3px solid #444; border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px 40px; text-align: center; font-size: 1.4em;"}
£1.30
:::
:::
:::

## Building the price relative {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:100px;"}
$$R^{0,t} = \frac{p^t}{p^0} = \frac{1.40}{1.30} = 1.0769$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.4em; margin-top:20px;"}
This ratio is called the **price relative**.
:::

## Turning the price relative into a percentage

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$\% \text{ change in price} = 100 \times (R^{0,t} - 1)$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$100 \times (1.0769 - 1) = 7.69\%$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We would say inflation between January and July 2014, for this one item, was
**7.69%**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="border-left: 6px solid #b03; padding-left: 20px;"}
A note: the printed textbook states this example works out to 8.33%. It does not.
Recomputed from its own numbers, £1.30 to £1.40 gives 7.69%, not 8.33%. This looks
like an arithmetic slip in the book itself, worth mentioning if a student checks the
original page.
:::

## From one item to a whole basket

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Now imagine $N$ items in a basket, not just one. Each item $i$ has its own price
relative.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$R_i^{0,t} = \frac{p_i^t}{p_i^0}$$
:::

## Worked example: five drinks

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Drink | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bitter (pint) | 1.95 | 1.80 | 2.00 |
| Lager (pint) | 2.40 | 2.65 | 2.60 |
| Wine (large glass) | 3.50 | 3.50 | 3.50 |
| Vodka (single) | 2.20 | 2.25 | 2.30 |
| Lemonade (half pint) | 0.80 | 0.90 | 0.95 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Bitter, 2012 to 2014: $\dfrac{2.00}{1.95} = 1.026$, up 2.6%.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Vodka, 2012 to 2013: $\dfrac{2.25}{2.20} = 1.023$, up 2.3%.
:::

## 4.2 Simple, un-weighted indices for price change {.center}

## The next question

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We can now find a price relative for any single item. But a real price index needs
to summarise *all five* drinks in **one** number.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This fixed collection of items is called a **basket of goods and services**. A
shopping basket that we track, month after month.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The UK CPI basket, for example, includes milk, bread, bacon and beer. It also
includes gas and electricity bills, fridges, cars, holidays, and even concert
tickets.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
So, with five price relatives in hand, how do we combine them into one?
:::

## Method 1: just average them

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The simplest idea. Add up the price relatives, divide by how many there are. The
plain arithmetic mean.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is called the **Carli** index.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Carli}} = 100 \times \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i^{0,t}$$
:::

## Method 2: average them multiplicatively

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Instead of adding the relatives, multiply them together, then take the $n$-th root.
The geometric mean.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is called the **Jevons** index.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Jevons}} = 100 \times \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} R_i^{0,t}\right)^{1/n}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Intuition: a price that doubles and a price that halves cancel out exactly under
Jevons. Under Carli, they do not.
:::

## Method 3: average the prices first

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Instead of averaging the *relatives*, average the raw prices in each period first,
then take the ratio of those two averages.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is called the **Dutot** index.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Dutot}} = 100 \times \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum p_i^t}{\frac{1}{n}\sum p_i^0}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Dutot silently gives more influence to items with a **higher price**, since it
averages pounds and pence, not ratios.
:::

## Method 4: the harmonic mean

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A less obvious average. Take the reciprocal of each price relative, average those,
then take the reciprocal of the result.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is the **Harmonic** index.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Harmonic}} = 100 \times \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{R_i^{0,t}}}$$
:::

## Method 5: split the difference

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Carli tends to sit a little high. Harmonic tends to sit a little low. Why not
average the two?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The **CSWD** index (Carruthers, Selwood, Ward and Dalen) is the geometric mean of
Carli and Harmonic.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{CSWD}} = \sqrt{P^{0,t}_{\text{Carli}} \times P^{0,t}_{\text{Harmonic}}}$$
:::

## Same data, five different answers

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Price relatives for the five drinks, 2012 to 2013: 0.923, 1.104, 1.000, 1.023, 1.125.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Method | Index value |
|---|---|
| Carli | 103.5 |
| Jevons | 103.2 |
| Dutot | 102.3 |
| Harmonic | 103.0 |
| CSWD | 103.2 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The estimate of inflation ranges from **2.3% to 3.5%**, using the exact same price
data. The choice of formula is not a technicality. It changes the answer.
:::

## 4.2.2 Simple quantity indices {.center}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Every one of the five formulas we just saw has an exact mirror image for
**quantities**. Just replace each price relative with a quantity relative.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$\tilde{R}_i^{0,t} = \frac{q_i^t}{q_i^0}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Carli, Jevons, Dutot, Harmonic, and CSWD all work exactly the same way, just applied
to quantities bought instead of prices paid.
:::

## 4.3 Price, quantity and value {.center}

## The relationship at the heart of it all

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Price, quantity, and value are linked in the simplest possible way.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$\text{value} = \text{price} \times \text{quantity}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
For a whole basket of $n$ items, the total value at period $t$ is:
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$V^t = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i^t q_i^t$$
:::

## What drives a change in value?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$V^{0,t} = \frac{\sum p_i^t q_i^t}{\sum p_i^0 q_i^0}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
If your weekly shopping bill goes up, is it because prices rose, because you bought
more, or some mix of both?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Price change and quantity change are often tangled together. In fact, they are
usually negatively related. When something gets pricier, people tend to buy less of
it.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Untangling this is exactly the problem the next chapter solves.
:::

# Part 4: Chapter 5, Laspeyres and Paasche Indices

## A fruit basket, three items

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Fruit | 2012 price | 2013 price | Price relative |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apples | £0.40 | £0.42 | 1.050 |
| Bananas | £0.50 | £0.55 | 1.100 |
| Pineapple | £1.25 | £2.00 | 1.600 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Apples rose 5%. Bananas rose 10%. Pineapples rose a dramatic 60%.
:::

## Combining them the old way

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Using three of the five formulas from Chapter 4:
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| Method | 2013 index |
|---|---|
| Carli | 125.0 |
| Dutot | 138.1 |
| Jevons | 122.7 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Every one of these answers is dragged upward by the pineapple's huge price jump.
:::

## But is that fair?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
In 2012, this basket actually contained **220 apples**, **230 bananas**, and just
**50 pineapples**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Pineapples were a small part of what people actually bought. Should their 60% jump
really dominate the overall answer, as much as it just did?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We are missing a crucial ingredient. **How much of each item was actually bought.**
:::

## 5.1 The Laspeyres price index {.center}

## The idea

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
What if we weight each item's price change by how much of it we bought, back in the
**base period**?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
That is exactly the **Laspeyres price index**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
It answers a very specific question. How has the cost of this basket changed, if I
buy the *same quantities* as I did in the base period?
:::

## The formula {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:100px;"}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Laspeyres}} = 100 \times \frac{\sum p_i^t q_i^0}{\sum p_i^0 q_i^0}$$
:::

## The formula {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:60px;"}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Laspeyres}} = 100 \times \frac{\sum p_i^t q_i^0}{\sum p_i^0 q_i^0}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.3em; margin-top:20px;"}
Notice the quantity term, $q^0$, is the **same in top and bottom**. Only price
changes. Quantities are frozen at base-period levels.
:::

## Calculating it for the fruit basket

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Top: $(0.42\times220) + (0.55\times230) + (2.00\times50) = 319$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Bottom: $(0.40\times220) + (0.50\times230) + (1.25\times50) = 266$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$100 \times \frac{319}{266} = 120.1$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Compare this to Carli's 125.0, Jevons's 122.7, and Dutot's 138.1. Weighting by real
quantities pulled the answer down, because pineapples matter less than their price
jump alone suggested.
:::

## 5.2 The Paasche price index {.center}

## A different, equally valid choice

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Laspeyres freezes quantities at the base period. But why the base period, and not
the current one?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
There is no obvious theoretical reason to prefer one over the other.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The **Paasche price index** freezes quantities at the **current** period instead.
:::

## The formula {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:100px;"}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Paasche}} = 100 \times \frac{\sum p_i^t q_i^t}{\sum p_i^0 q_i^t}$$
:::

## The formula {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:60px;"}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Paasche}} = 100 \times \frac{\sum p_i^t q_i^t}{\sum p_i^0 q_i^t}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.3em; margin-top:20px;"}
This time $q^t$, the **current** quantity, appears in both top and bottom.
:::

## Calculating it for the fruit basket

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
By 2013, quantities sold had shifted. 300 apples, only 170 bananas, and just 30
pineapples.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Top: $(0.42\times300) + (0.55\times170) + (2.00\times30) = 279.5$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Bottom: $(0.40\times300) + (0.50\times170) + (1.25\times30) = 242.5$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$100 \times \frac{279.5}{242.5} = 115.3$$
:::

## Ranking every answer we now have

::: {.incremental}
- Paasche: 115.3
- Laspeyres: 120.1
- Jevons: 122.7
- Carli: 125.0
- Dutot: 138.1
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Same underlying prices. Five different pictures of "how much did prices rise."
:::

## 5.3 Laspeyres and Paasche quantity indices {.center}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Just as with the simple indices, both formulas have quantity-index mirror images.
Swap the roles of price and quantity.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$Q^{0,t}_{\text{Laspeyres}} = 100 \times \frac{\sum p_i^0 q_i^t}{\sum p_i^0 q_i^0}
\qquad
Q^{0,t}_{\text{Paasche}} = 100 \times \frac{\sum p_i^t q_i^t}{\sum p_i^t q_i^0}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A worked DIY-tools example in the book (screwdrivers, drills, ladders, hammers,
saws) gives Laspeyres price 110.2, Paasche price 110.3, and both quantity indices
96.6.
:::

## 5.4 Laspeyres and Paasche: mind your Ps and Qs {.center}

## A more useful way to write Laspeyres

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The Laspeyres formula can be rewritten using only price relatives and **value
shares**. In practice, this form is far more common.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Laspeyres}} = 100 \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i^{0,t} \cdot s_i^0$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Here $s_i^0$ is item $i$'s **share of total spending** in the base period.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is a **weighted average of price relatives**, where the weight is exactly how
much of the household budget went on that item.
:::

## And the Paasche version

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Paasche has the same intuition, but with a twist. It is a weighted **harmonic**
mean, not a weighted arithmetic mean, using **current-period** value shares.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P^{0,t}_{\text{Paasche}} = 100 \times \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{s_i^t}{R_i^{0,t}}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The same asymmetry we saw in Chapter 4, arithmetic mean versus harmonic mean, shows
up again here.
:::

## 5.5 Laspeyres, Paasche and the Index Number Problem {.center}

## A problem worth naming

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
> **The Index Number Problem.** How to combine the relative changes in the prices
> and quantities of various products into a single measure of the relative change of
> the overall price level, and a single measure of the relative change of the
> overall quantity level.
>
> *(OECD definition)*
:::

## A neat solution

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The total change in value can always be split into a price part and a quantity
part.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$V^{0,t} = P^{0,t}_{\text{Laspeyres}} \times Q^{0,t}_{\text{Paasche}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$V^{0,t} = P^{0,t}_{\text{Paasche}} \times Q^{0,t}_{\text{Laspeyres}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Laspeyres and Paasche fit together perfectly to solve the Index Number Problem, as
long as you pair a price index with the *opposite* quantity index.
:::

## 5.6 Laspeyres or Paasche? {.center}

## The practical trade-off

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**Laspeyres** only needs quantity data from one period, the base period. That makes
it cheap and quick to calculate every month.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**Paasche** needs fresh quantity data in *every* period. That is expensive, slow,
and often simply not available in time.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
But Laspeyres pays a price for that convenience. It can go out of date, since it
never updates to reflect changing buying habits.
:::

## When the two can diverge sharply

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A supermarket sells two nearly identical coffee brands. In January, both cost
**£2.50**, and 500 jars of each were sold.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
In February, Brand A rises to £4.00. Brand B stays at £2.50. Shoppers notice, and
switch. Only 100 jars of A sell, but 900 jars of B.
:::

## Two very different answers

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Laspeyres, using January's equal 500/500 split as weights:
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$100 \times \frac{(4.00\times500)+(2.50\times500)}{(2.50\times500)+(2.50\times500)} = 130.0$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Paasche, using February's actual 100/900 split:
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$100 \times \frac{(4.00\times100)+(2.50\times900)}{(2.50\times100)+(2.50\times900)} = 106.0$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Laspeyres overstates the price rise, since it ignores the switch to Brand B.
Paasche understates it, since it barely weights Brand A's big price jump at all.
:::

## 5.7 A more practical alternative {.center}

## Neither base period nor current period

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
What if we fix quantities at some *other* period, $b$, ideally a bit before the base
period, giving statisticians time to actually collect reliable weight data?
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
This is the **Lowe index**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
$$P_{\text{Lowe}} = \frac{\sum p_i^t q_i^b}{\sum p_i^0 q_i^b}$$
:::

## The fact that matters most today

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {style="font-size: 1.3em; border-left: 6px solid #b03; padding-left: 20px;"}
Almost every National Statistical Institute in the world, including the one that
compiles India's CPI, actually uses the Lowe index, not a pure Laspeyres or Paasche
index.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Laspeyres and Paasche are the special cases. Real statistical offices sit in
between, using older, reliable weights.
:::

## 5.8 Chapter summary {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- Chapter 4's simple indices ignore quantities entirely, and can be dominated by one
  volatile item.
- Laspeyres and Paasche fix that, by weighting price relatives with quantities, from
  the base period or the current period respectively.
- Neither is perfect. Laspeyres is cheap but can go stale. Paasche is current but
  expensive to collect.
- In practice, real statistical offices use the Lowe index, a practical compromise
  between the two.
:::

# Part 5: Case Study, Compiling India's CPI

## From the book to the real thing {.center}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Basket, price relatives, weights, Laspeyres-type aggregation. Every mechanism from
today is at work, every single month, in India's actual Consumer Price Index.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We now look at how the National Statistical Office builds it, and what happened when
the COVID-19 lockdown broke the normal process.
:::

## Who builds India's CPI?

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The **National Statistical Office (NSO)**, under the Ministry of Statistics and
Programme Implementation, compiles All-India and state-wise CPI.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
It covers **Rural**, **Urban**, and **Combined** sectors, and is released on the
12th of every month.
:::

## Where the raw prices come from

::: {.incremental}
- Monthly price data comes from **1,114 selected urban markets** and **1,181
  selected villages**.
- Field staff collect it through personal visits, on a weekly roster.
- Prices are uploaded, then scrutinised and validated centrally before they enter
  the index.
:::

## The CPI's basket structure {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.6em; margin-top:60px;"}
Items build sub-groups. Sub-groups build groups. Groups build the General Index.
:::

## The CPI's basket structure {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.3em; margin-top:20px;"}
Items build sub-groups. Sub-groups build groups. Groups build the General Index.
:::

::: {.incremental style="margin-top:30px; font-size:1.1em;"}
- Six major groups. Food and beverages, Clothing and footwear, Housing, Fuel and
  light, Pan, tobacco and intoxicants, and Miscellaneous.
- These break into 23 sub-groups, such as Cereals, Vegetables, Clothing, Health, and
  Transport.
- Each carries its own weight, estimated separately for Rural, Urban, and Combined.
:::

## Where each chapter shows up in practice

::: {.incremental}
- **Elementary indices.** Multiple price quotes for one good are combined with a
  simple geometric mean. This is the Jevons method from Chapter 4.
- **Aggregation.** Elementary indices combine into sub-group and group indices using
  expenditure weights. This is the Laspeyres-type, Lowe-style logic from Chapter 5.
:::

## From state to national indices

::: {.incremental}
- This is done first for each State and Union Territory, separately for Rural,
  Urban, and Combined.
- All-India indices are then built by aggregating the weighted State and UT
  indices.
:::

## A worked example: reading the real numbers

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
India's CPI, Combined, base 2012 equals 100.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| | April 2020 | May 2020 |
|---|---|---|
| **General Index (All Groups)** | 151.4 | 150.9 |
| **Food & Beverages** | 154.0 | 152.7 |
| **Housing** | 155.6 | 155.6 |
| **Fuel and light** | 144.1 | 142.5 |
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Overall prices were about 51% above 2012 levels in April, easing slightly in May.
Housing stayed flat while fuel prices fell.
:::

## When the machine breaks

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The nation-wide COVID-19 lockdown made it infeasible for field staff to visit retail
outlets and collect price quotations.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Market transactions were themselves limited. Many items simply were not being bought
and sold as usual.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Price data on all commodities was not available. Of 23 sub-groups, only 13 could be
compiled for April 2020, and only 15 for May 2020.
:::

## What the international community said

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
NSO consulted the World Bank, ILO, ADB, IMF, Eurostat, OECD, and others through the
Inter-Secretariat Working Group on Price Statistics.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="border-left: 6px solid #b03; padding-left:20px;"}
Their guidance: if a whole index is missing, impute it using the next level up. If
oranges are missing, use the citrus index, and so on up to the all-items index.
:::

## Imputation, the general idea {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:100px;"}
::: {.r-fit-text}
If it is missing, estimate it from what you do know.
:::
:::

## Micro-level imputation

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
A **temporarily missing** individual price is estimated from last month's price for
that same item.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
It is adjusted by the average price movement seen in the quotations that are still
available. Same logic as the elementary aggregates in Chapter 4.
:::

## Macro-level imputation

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
An **entire missing** sub-group or group index is estimated using the movement of
the next level up that could still be calculated.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The parent is the Food and Beverages Group index for food sub-groups. It is the
General CPI itself for non-food sub-groups.
:::

## Macro imputation, built step by step {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.5em; margin-top:60px;"}
Last known index of the missing sub-group
:::

## Macro imputation, built step by step {auto-animate="true"}

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.4em; margin-top:40px;"}
Last known index, multiplied by how much the parent index moved
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; margin-top:40px; font-size:1.2em;"}
Parent is Food & Beverages Group, if the sub-group is a food item
:::
::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.2em;"}
Parent is General CPI, if the sub-group is a non-food item
:::

## Worked example: prepared meals, snacks, sweets

::: {.incremental}
- Last observed index, March 2020: **160.0**
- Food & Beverages Group index, April 2020: **150.1**
- Food & Beverages Group index, March 2020: **148.2**
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.5em; margin-top:30px;"}
160.0 × (150.1 ÷ 148.2) = **162.1**, the imputed April index
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="border-left: 6px solid #b03; padding-left: 20px; font-size: 0.9em;"}
The NSO's own published note states 162.2 here. Recomputed from the published
150.1 and 148.2, the arithmetic gives 162.05, which rounds to 162.1. The likely
cause: the Food & Beverages index is published to one decimal place, but the actual
imputation was almost certainly run on unrounded internal figures.
:::

## Worked example: clothing

::: {.incremental}
- Last observed index, March 2020: **153.4**
- General CPI, April 2020: **150.3**
- General CPI, March 2020: **149.8**
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up style="text-align:center; font-size:1.5em; margin-top:30px;"}
153.4 × (150.3 ÷ 149.8) = **153.9**, the imputed April index
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
The logic is identical to the meals example. Only the parent index changes, since
clothing is a non-food item.
:::

## After imputation

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Once every missing sub-group is filled this way, the General CPI is recalculated for
all 23 sub-groups.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
NSO flagged every imputed cell in its published tables. It described the series as a
business-continuity estimate, not an ordinary observed index.
:::

## Why this matters beyond statistics class

::: {.incremental}
- Any wage revision or contract that referenced CPI in April and May 2020 was partly
  relying on an estimated number.
- Building an index, and patching it when data fails, involves judgment calls with
  real distributive consequences.
- This is the same "small rule, big pattern" idea this course keeps returning to.
:::

# Wrap-up

## Key takeaways: Chapters 1 and 2

::: {.incremental}
- An index number rescales a series so change is easy to read, anchored at a base
  period.
- The same construction, raw data combined into one number, shows up in the CPI,
  the FTSE 100, and composite indicators like the MPI.
- Index numbers make comparison across very different scales possible.
:::

## Key takeaways: Chapters 4 and 5

::: {.incremental}
- Combining many price relatives into one number is not automatic. Five different
  averaging methods give five different answers, from the same data.
- Weighting by quantities, Laspeyres or Paasche, fixes the biggest weakness of
  unweighted indices.
- Real statistical offices use a practical compromise, the Lowe index.
:::

## Key takeaways: the case study

::: {.incremental}
- India's CPI applies every one of these mechanisms every month, at national scale.
- When normal data collection broke down in 2020, the same underlying logic kept the
  series alive.
- Borrow information from the next level up, transparently, using clearly stated
  formulas.
:::

From measuring prices, to measuring everything else
